title: Tradescantia pallida

{{Short description|Species of flowering plant}} {{ntbcw|Tradescantia zebrina}} {{Speciesbox | image = Trapoeraba-roxa (do tupi *tarapoeraba) em Bagé, RS, Brasil - 55378584901.jpg | image_caption = ''Tradescantia pallida'' 'Purpurea' | genus = Tradescantia | species = pallida | authority = ([[Joseph Nelson Rose|Rose]]) [[David Hunt (botanist)|D.R.Hunt]] | synonyms = ''Setcreasea pallida'' Rose
''Setcreasea purpurea'' Boom | synonyms_ref = {{GRIN | accessdate=2011-11-20}} }} '''''Tradescantia pallida''''' is a species of [[spiderwort]] native to the [[Gulf Coast of Mexico|Gulf Coast region]] of eastern [[Mexico]]. It is a [[perennial]] [[herbaceous]] species with a trailing [[plant habit|habit]]. The cultivar ''T. pallida'' 'Purpurea', commonly called '''purple heart''' or '''purple queen''' or '''wandering Jew''', is widely grown as a [[houseplant]], outdoor [[container garden|container]] plant, or a garden [[groundcover]]. The species has been proven useful in [[biomonitoring|indicating]] and [[phytoremediation|removing]] air and soil pollutants and has also been used in [[food technology]]. ==Taxonomy== ''T. pallida'' is a species of [[spiderwort]] in the family [[Commelinaceae]]. The [[type specimen]] was collected by [[Edward Palmer (botanist)|Edward Palmer]], one of the main US [[plant collector]]s of his time, in the [[Mexican state]] of [[Tamaulipas]] (possibly near [[Ciudad Victoria]]) in 1907.{{cite web|first=Gerald|last=Klingaman|title=Plant of the Week: ''Tradescantia pallida'', Purple Heart|url=https://www.uaex.uada.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/Tradescantia-pallida-Purple-Heart-10-21-2016.aspx|publisher=University of Arkansas|date=21 October 2016|access-date = 29 September 2024}} The species was [[species description|described]] by [[Joseph Nelson Rose]] in 1911. He placed it in the [[genus]] ''[[Setcreasea]]''. In 1975 [[David Hunt (botanist)|David Hunt]] transferred the species to the genus ''[[Tradescantia]]''.{{cite web|first=Susan|last=Mahr|title=Purple Heart, ''Tradescantia pallida''|url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/purple-heart-tradescantia-pallida/|publisher=University of Wisconsin|date=|access-date=29 September 2024}} Hunt also treated ''Setcreasea purpurea'' as a [[cultivar]] of ''S. pallida''.{{cite journal|last1=Hunt |first1=D. R. |title= The Reunion of ''Setcreasea'' and ''Separotheca'' with ''Tradescantia'' American ''Commelinaceae'': I|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4103068|volume=30|number=3|year=1975|pages=443–458|journal=Kew Bulletin|doi=10.2307/4103068 |jstor=4103068 |bibcode=1975KewBu..30..443H |access-date=29 September 2024|url-access=subscription}} The latter names are still often used to refer to ''T. pallida''. The [[specific epithet]] ''pallida'' means "pale", referring to the original color of the leaves. The plant is known by several [[common name]]s, including purple heart (probably in reference to the [[Purple Heart|eponymous military medal]]) and purple wandering jew. ==Description== ''T. pallida'' is [[perennial]] and [[herbaceous]]. It has a rambling [[plant habit|habit]], with plants reaching about a {{cvt|1|ft|cm}} in height but spreading considerably wider: the stems may trail to {{cvt|18|in|cm}} or more. Wild specimens are gray-green-purplish with a washed out look. [[File:Tradescantia pallida flower.jpg|thumb|left|Flower of ''T. pallida'' 'Purpurea']] The fleshy, hairy leaves are up to {{cvt|7|in}} long, narrow-oblong, and v-shaped. and form a sheath around fleshy stems, which break off easily. On the ends of the stems the plants produce relatively inconspicuous flowers. The flowers are three-[[petal]]ed as is typical for the ''Tradescantia'' genus. The flowering is most abundant from midsummer through fall and sporadic at other times of the year. The flowers are open only in the morning. The plants are [[evergreen]], but in colder areas [[deciduous|die back]] to the ground in winter and resprout from the roots in spring. ==Distribution and habitat== ''T. pallida'' is found along the coast of the [[Gulf of Mexico]]. Its [[native range]] extends from Tamaulipas to [[Yucatan]]. The species has been collected in a [[tropical deciduous forest]], among roadside [[limestone]] rocks, and on limestone [[outcrops]]. ==Uses== [[File:Tradeskansia.jpg|thumb|''T. pallida'' 'Purpurea' as a houseplant]] ''T. pallida'' is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] for its attractive foliage. Only the [[cultivar]] 'Purpurea', featuring purple-violet leaves and stems,{{cite web|title=Tradescantia pallida 'Purpurea'|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=c137|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden|access-date=29 September 2024}} is commercially grown. 'Purpurea' is sometimes sold under the name 'Purple Heart', and has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web|title = ''Tradescantia pallida'' 'Purpurea' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/18297/Tradescantia-pallida-Purpurea/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}} ''T. pallida'' is a popular [[groundcover]] plant in [[tropical]] and [[semi-tropical]] areas. In [[temperate climate]]s it has traditionally been used as a [[houseplant]] but is increasingly being planted outdoors in [[container garden|containers]] or as a groundcover. It is also suitable for [[hanging basket]]s, [[perennial border|border]] fronts, and [[rock garden]]s. The plant is [[plant hardiness|hardy]] down to [[USDA zone]] 7. It may be grown in the shade but the most intense purple color is achieved in full sun. The plant is remarkable for easily tolerating both drought and frequent watering. It is generally not affected by [[plant pest|pests]] or [[plant disease|diseases]]; however, slugs and caterpillars may attack young shoots of outdoor specimens, while houseplants should be monitored for [[aphid]]s and [[scale insect|scale]]. ''T. pallida'' has been proven useful for [[phytoremediation]], [[biomonitoring]], and [[genotoxicity]] assessment of [[environmental pollutants]], especially [[heavy metals]] and [[metalloid]]s from [[coal power plant]]s.{{cite journal|first1=Neelima|last1=Meravi|first2=Santosh Kumar|last2=Prajapati|title=Biomonitoring the Genotoxicity of Heavy Metals/Metalloids Present in Soil Contaminated by Fly Ash from Coal-Fired Thermal Power Plant Using Tradescantia pallida|journal=Phytoremediation|volume=1|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3319103952|year=2014|page=173}} As a houseplant, ''T. pallida'' has been judged exceptionally effective at improving [[indoor air quality]] by filtering out [[volatile organic compounds]], a class of common pollutants and respiratory irritants.{{cite journal|last1=Yang|first1=Dong Sik|last2=Pennisi|first2=Svoboda V.|last3=Son|first3=Ki-Cheol|last4=Kays|first4=Stanley J.|title=Screening Indoor Plants for Volatile Organic Pollutant Removal Efficiency|journal=HortScience|date=1 August 2009|volume=44|issue=5|pages=1377–1381|doi=10.21273/HORTSCI.44.5.1377 |doi-access=free}} Because the plant contains [[anthocyanin]]s, ''T. pallida'' leaves have been used as [[food colorant]]s{{cite book|first1=J.D.|last1=Houghton|first2=G.A.F.|last2=Hendry|title=Natural Food Colorants|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|year=2012|isbn=978-1461521556}} and [[food preservative]]s.{{cite journal|first1=Fariha|last1=Imtiaz|first2=Muhammad|last2=Islam|first3=Hamid|last3=Saeed|first4=Abrar|last4=Ahmed|first5=Hassaan
